title: 101 Zen Stories, Part 1: Japanese Zen Stories
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Nyogen Senzaki's 1919 collection 101 Zen Stories, reading from its first half to show how Zen stories look once they move from Chinese koans into Japan. Nomon tells the stories of Nanin's overflowing teacup, Hakuen's "Is that so?", Tanzan carrying the girl across the mud, and Chiyono's pail with no bottom. Nomon adds Soyen Shaku's daily rules ("the fearless attitude of a hero and the loving heart of a child") and Bankei keeping the thief in sesshin. A sidebar on Paul Reps and his line "Drinking a cup of tea, I stopped the war" opens the evening. Participants close by trading family stories, including one about a child who thinks the moon is following the car because it wants some of the chicken.

sentences.text: Well, we recently finished going through a whole bunch of the formal Zen koans in one of the formal collections, as you know, the Nomon koan.
I want to share that I'm working on getting the dharma talks on the website better organized.
Next time you go on the website, take a look at the dharma talks page under teachings.
I'm starting to break out categories.
So far it's just been this scroll through time, and after a certain number of weeks, they disappear into the mist.
So I made a page for all the Nomon koan talks, so you can re-listen to your favorites, or maybe you missed them.
There are other categories too: Buddhist basics, the talks on the chant book.
It's halfway done, but you'll see the structure, and that should make the talks a lot easier to find later.
And Ken, maybe I'll bug you at some point, and we can figure out a way to collaborate on doing that as we go, once I get it caught up.
The formal koans in the Nomon koan are all about the Chinese Chan masters.
The school was called Chan, not Zen, in China.
It's just the pronunciation of the same character in Chinese versus the way the Japanese say it.
And it's all from that golden age of Zen.
Every religion, every tradition has its golden age, it seems like.
In this case, the golden age is the seventh through the ninth or tenth centuries.
Then in the 11th and 12th centuries, they wrote about it and decided it was the golden age.
But a lot of Zen stories that get passed around and talked about and pop up in dharma talks are actually about figures in Japan.
So I was wondering where those are collected.
Are they just word of mouth?
How do we know?
Are they really official stories?
I was poking around and I discovered that my good buddy Nyogen Senzaki, remember, one of the earliest Japanese teachers in America, came to America with his teacher, Soyen Shaku, in 1905, I think.
He was the one who just stayed, with no real plan.
Somehow he made it work, totally alone in this foreign land with minimal English.
It turns out Nyogen Senzaki published a collection called *101 Zen Stories* in 1919.
I couldn't find out, but it might be the first book in English on Zen, actually, published by this quirky, independent priest trying to make his way in America.
He must have learned enough English by 1919 to write it.
I learned it was partly a translation of a set of Japanese stories that were written down in the 13th century, so it's only a little bit later than these famous koan collections.
But a lot of them he added, and there are no footnotes, and he doesn't explain where he got them from.
A few of them are actually about his teacher, so we know that he wrote those ones.
But I suspect it was him writing down the stories he had heard in the monastery.
He was a monastic from a young age.
And just like us with any stories, all stories get passed around.
Later, most of these stories, maybe all of them, were included in a book written by a poet and raconteur named Paul Reps.
That book, called Zen Flesh, Zen Bones, was quite well known, published in the 50s, the late 50s.
But I doubt much of anybody ever heard of this book by Nyogen Senzaki published in 1919.
I suspect it was a very small press and a limited run, or maybe he self-published it, who knows.
I really don't know the history of the text.
But it's fun to remember that the pre-internet age was like that, right?
It could be this obscure book that's in a few bookstores and a few people's collections.
You had to hunt and call antique bookstores to find it.
People would fly around to different cities hunting for a book.
Tragically, now it's all on Amazon.
The hunt is over.
So Paul Reps is kind of funny.

Here's a sidebar about Paul Reps, and then I want to dive into a few of these stories, because it fleshes out the idea of Zen stories a little bit beyond the formal koans, which are about these Chinese masters, and brings it forward into Japan.
The Japanese are a different culture, right?
So they have a different style than in China.
Anyway, here's a little story about Paul Reps.
According to Steven Levine, during the Korean War, Reps traveled to Japan to see one of his Zen masters; he'd somehow established a Zen practice.
Steven Levine, who's recounting the story, says that at that time you couldn't just go to Japan.
It was a staging place for the Korean War.
An immigration officer said to Paul Reps, "You can't come in now.
The country is not open to American travelers."
So Paul took his immigration papers, the application he had written, turned it over, and wrote on the back of it, "Drinking a cup of tea, I stopped the war," and handed it to the immigration officer.
The immigration officer looked at it and said, "Er, yes, we need more people like you in Japan," and a lot of men.
So that's a sidebar story about Paul Reps.
I don't know where he got this line, "Drinking a cup of tea, I stopped the war."
But I remember there was an art piece at Green Gulch Farm Zen Center that had that quotation in it, so maybe that came from the story.
A wonderful Zen sentiment, isn't it?
To stop a war, drink a cup of tea.
Tonight I just want to share a few of the stories from Nyogen Senzaki's collection from 1919, *101 Zen Stories*, that I find interesting and had never heard of.
I got through the first half of the book.
If you're not too bored with these, I'll do the second half of the book next week, and then I promise we'll move on to something else, beyond Zen stories and koans.
But they give you a flavor of Zen as it moves through Japan.
Story one: "A Cup of Tea," Nanin.
*A cup of tea.
Nanin, a Japanese master during the Meiji era, 1880s-ish, received a university professor who came to inquire about Zen.
Nanin served tea.
He poured the visitor's cup full, and then kept on pouring.
The professor watched the overflow until he could no longer restrain himself.
"It's overfull.
No more can go in."
"Ah, like this cup," Nanin said.
"You are full of your own opinions and speculations.
How can I show you Zen unless you first empty your cup?"*
So you may have heard that story before.
But yeah, here it is, written down, long 1919.
So is your cup full or empty when you come to practice, when you show up for a day of your life, when you meet somebody?
Is your cup full of knowing who they are and what they're going to say, right?
Or can it be more empty, more open?
Beautiful metaphor.
Story three is a very famous story, which I have repeated several times.
It's a little borderline sexist, as some of these are, but it's a famous story, so it's worth sharing.
The title of the story in his book is "Is That So?"
*The Zen master Hakuen was praised by his neighbors as one living a pure life.
Then a beautiful Japanese girl whose parents owned a food store near him.
Suddenly, without warning, her parents discovered that she was a child.
This made her parents very angry and she would not confess who the man was.
But after much harassment, at last she named Hakuen.
In great anger, the parents went to the master with the baby.*
I didn't read this out loud, and now I noticed that Nyogen Senzaki sometimes leaves out a few words, so maybe his English was still under development.
So I'll try not to fill in too much.
We get the gist, I think.
Anyway, the way it's written is they went to the master, and "holding the baby" is the part left out.
*"Is that so?" was all he would say.*
And because the child hasn't been born yet, so they went to the master to complain.
*"Is that so?" was all he would say.
And after the child was born, it was brought to Hakuen.
And by this time he had lost his reputation, which did not trouble him.
But he took good care of the child.
He obtained milk from his neighbors and everything else the little one needed.
But a year later, the girl mother could stand it no longer.
She told her parents the truth.
That the real father of the child was a young man who worked in the fish market.
The mother and father of the girl at once went to Hakuen to beg his forgiveness, to apologize at length, and get the child back again.
Hakuen was willing.
Yielding the child, all he said was, "Is that so?"*
And "is that so" is a translation of one of the few phrases I know in Japanese.
It's just a phrase people use constantly there, which is "sou desu," or "sou desuka."
You can picture him saying, "Oh, sou desu."
Is that so?
Sou desu.
So, a quirky story about acceptance, right?
And about reputation.

It refers also to the so-called eight worldly winds in early Buddhism, which encourage us not to get so worried about praise instead of blame, about a good reputation instead of a bad reputation, about everything going well, everything going poorly.
And who really knows what good or bad is, ultimately?
So can we accept even the insults and misunderstandings and trials and tribulations with an open heart, with acceptance?
Receiving the baby, giving the baby away.
So, is that so?
Story four, "Obedience."
*Zen master Bankei is a famous 18th century Zen master.
Zen master Bankei's talks were attended not only by Zen students, but by persons of all ranks and sects.
He never quoted sutras or indulged in scholastic dissertations.
Instead, his words are spoken directly from his heart to the hearts of his listeners.
His large audiences angered a priest of the Nichiren sect because the adherents had left to hear about Zen from Bankei.
In the self-centered Nichiren, Zen-oh school of Buddhism, the self-centered Nichiren priest came to the temple determined to debate with Bankei.
"Hey, Zen teacher," he called out.
"Wait a minute, whoever respects you will obey what you say.
But a man like yourself, but a man like myself does not respect you.
Can you make me obey you?"*
So the rival teacher says, *"Hey Zen teacher, wait a minute, whoever respects you will obey what you say.
But a man like myself does not respect you.
Can you make me obey you?"
"Come up beside me and I'll show you," said Bankei.
Proudly the priest pushed through the crowd to the teacher.
Bankei smiled.
"Come over to my left side."
The priest obeyed.
"No," the priest proudly stepped over to the right.
"You see," observed Bankei, "you're obeying me and I think you're a very gentle person.
Now sit down and listen."*
So there was intersect rivalry, I guess, is the point.
Pride, you know, we would be free from pride.
Some of them are just quirky.
Story seven, "Announcement."
*Tanzan wrote 60 postal cards on the last day of his life and asked an attendant to mail them.
Then he passed away.
The cards read, "I am departing from this world.
This is my last announcement.
Tanzan, July 27, 1892."*
This is a famous thing in Zen, to predict when you're going to die and have your last words ready to go.
"I'm departing from this world.
This is my last announcement."
Story nine, "The Moon Cannot Be Stolen."
*Ryokan, a Zen master and a poet, lived the simplest kind of life in a little hut at the foot of the mountain.
One evening, a thief visited the hut, only to discover there was nothing in it to steal.
Ryokan returned and caught him.
"Oh, you have come a long way to visit me," he told the prowler.
"And you should not return empty handed.
Please take my clothes as a gift."
The thief was bewildered, but he took the clothes and slunk away.
Ryokan sat down naked, watching the moon.
"Poor fellow," he mused.
"I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon."*
A lot of stories about Ryokan.
Also 18th century, maybe late 17th, I forget.
Chapter 14, another really famous one.
*Tanzan and Ikido were traveling together down a muddy road.
A heavy rain was falling.
Coming around a bend, they met a lovely girl in a silk kimono and a sash, unable to cross the intersection.
Too muddy.
"Come on, girl," said Tanzan at once, lifting her into his arms and carried her over the mud.
Ikido did not speak again until that night when they reached their lodging temple.
Then he could no longer restrain himself.
"We monks don't carry females," he told Tanzan, "especially not young and lovely ones.
It's dangerous.
It's bad for your practice.
Why did you do that?"
"Mmm," said Tanzan.
"I left the girl back there.
Why are you still carrying her?"*
Classic one, also a little sexist.
So, also talking about precepts, right?
How do we hold precepts?
Often it's described as three levels: literal level, compassionate level, and kind of absolute level.
So Tanzan on the compassionate level and Ikido on this literal level.
Kind of a strange misogynist precept, but Nonetheless, we get the point.
Story 18, a parable.
*Buddha told a parable in a sutra.
A man traveling across a field encountered a tiger.
He fled, the tiger after him.
Coming to a precipice, he caught hold of a root of a wild vine and swung himself over the ledge.
The tiger sniffed at him from above.
Trembling, the man looked down to where far below another tiger was waiting to eat him.
Only the vine sustained him.
Then two mice, one white and one black, little by little started to gnaw away the vine.
And the man saw a luscious strawberry near him.
Grasping the vine with one hand, he plucked the strawberry with the other.
How sweet it tasted.*
The white mouse and the black mouse are supposed to represent wholesome and unwholesome, good and evil.
Story 22 is actually about Nyogen Senzaki's teacher, Soin Shaku.
So he sprinkles stories about his teacher, maybe stuff he experienced himself, in his book.
This one he calls "My Heart Burns Like Fire."
*Soin Shaku, the first Zen teacher to come to America, said, "My heart burns like fire, but my eyes are as cold as dead ashes."
He made the following rules when he practiced every day of his life.
In the morning before dressing, light incense and meditate.
Retire at a regular hour.
Partake of food at regular intervals, eat with moderation, and never to the point of satisfaction.
Receive a guest with the same attitude you have when you are alone.
When alone, maintain the same attitude you have when receiving guests.
Watch what you say, and whatever you say, practice it.
When an opportunity comes, do not let it pass you by, yet always think twice before acting.
Do not regret the past.
Look to the future.
Have the fearless attitude of a hero and the loving heart of a child.
Upon retiring, sleep as if you had entered your last sleep.
Upon awakening, leave your bed behind you instantly, as if you have cast away a pair of old shoes.*
Soin Shaku's daily practice is described: be regular in your sleeping and your eating and your sitting.
This thing about guests is interesting.
So don't be too excited, or be equally excited whether you're with people or alone.
What's the real difference?
I love this part about the fearless attitude of a hero and the loving heart of a child.
Isn't that beautiful?
I'll practice that way.
Fearless attitude of a hero and the loving heart of a child.
And go to bed on time.
Get right up.
One thing that is kind of nice, though, is that Nyogen Senzaki did include stories of enlightened and awakened women.
Some of the stories in here ended up in Florence Capelot and Susan Moon's book, which I'm blanking the title of right now, but a wonderful book of koans on women teachers.
Oh, *Stories of the Hidden Lamp*.
*Stories of the Hidden Lamp.* So here's one of those.
Story 29, "No Water, No Moon."
*When the nun Chiyono studied Zen under Buko of Engaku, she was unable to attain the fruits of meditation for a long time.
At last, one moonlit night, she was carrying water in an old pail bound with bamboo.
The bamboo broke and the bottom fell out of the pail.
At that moment, Chiyono was set free.
In commemoration, she wrote a poem:*
*In this way that I tried to save the old pail, since the bamboo strip was weakening and about to break, until at last the bottom fell out.
No more water in the pail, no more moon in the water.*
So this is her enlightenment poem.
*In this way that I tried to save the old pail, since the bamboo strip was weakening and about to break, till at last the bottom fell out.
No more water in the pail, no more moon in the water.*
So the symbolism there is enlightenment.
The moon represents enlightenment.
And so how beautiful and wonderful to look in your pail of water when you're out at the well at night and see the moon reflected in the water.
Wow, right?
That seems pretty great.
But even better is when the bottom falls out.
Even better, beyond enlightenment: no moon in the water, no water at all.
There's some classic kind of stories about succession.
Here's one of them.
Story 34, "A Smile in His Lifetime."
*Mokugen was never known to smile as a teacher.
He was never known to smile until his last day on earth.
When his time came to pass away, he said to his faithful students, "You who have studied with me for more than ten years, show me your real interpretation of Zen.
Whoever expresses this most clearly shall be my successor and receive my robe and bowl."
Everyone watched Mokugen's severe face and no one could answer.
Then Incho, a disciple who'd been with his teacher for a really long time, moved to his bedside.
He pushed forward the medicine cup a few inches.
This was his answer to the command.
The teacher's face became even more severe and grave.
"Is that all you understand?" he asked.
Incho reached out and moved the cup back again.
And at that, a beautiful smile broke out over the features of Mokugen.
"You rascal," he told Incho.
"You worked with me ten years and have not yet seen my whole body.
Take the robe and bowl.
They belong to you."*

It's a lot of play, but play with a really long setup: ten, twenty years of never smiling or praising his students till the day of his death, when you can play with his chief student and enjoy each other.
Just a few more.
Here's another one about Nyogen's teacher, called "Sleeping in the Daytime."
*The master Soyanshaku passed from this world when he was 61 years of age.
Fulfilling his life's work, he left a great teaching, far richer than that of most Zen masters.
His pupils used to sleep in the daytime during midsummer, and while he overlooked this, he himself never wasted a minute.
When he was 12 years old, he was already studying Tendai philosophy.
And one summer day, the air had been so sultry that little Soyan stretched his legs and went to sleep while his teacher was away.
Three hours passed when suddenly waking, he heard his master enter, but it was too late.
There he lay, sprawled across the doorway.
"I beg your pardon.
I beg your pardon," his teacher whispered, stepping carefully over Soyan's body, as if he were that of some distinguished guest.
After that, Soyan never slept again in the afternoon.*
There's some Japanese cultural stuff there for sure: subtle ways of making suggestions.
Even though there's plenty of harshness and intensity in our tradition, there's also a wonderful kind of Japanese cultural norm of never correcting anybody directly.
You know, "Excuse me, you know, really meaning it.
I don't know how important that one was, but it's just interesting to hear some of these stories that Nyogen Senzaki put in there about his teacher.
What did he choose?
Let's do two more.
Try to decide which one.
Yeah, let's do this one.
*44, the thief who became a disciple.
One evening as Shichiri Kojin was reciting sutras, a thief with a sharp sword entered, demanding either his money or his life.
Shichiri told him, do not disturb me.
You can find the money in that drawer.
Then he resumed his recitation.
A little while afterwards, he stopped and called, don't take it all.
I need to pay taxes tomorrow.
The intruder gathered up most of the money and started to leave.
Thank a person when you receive a gift, Shichiri added.
So the thief thanked him and made off.
A few days afterwards, the fellow was caught and confessed [unclear: "among and confessed among others as offense"] against Shichiri.
Shichiri was called as a witness and he said, this man is no thief, at least as far as I'm concerned.
I gave him money and he thanked me for it.
And after he finished his prison term, the man went to Shichiri, became his disciple and studied Zen for the rest of his life.*
Yeah, one more, one last one.
This one is about Sangha life.
*Number 45, right and wrong.
When Bankei*, we heard about Bankei earlier, the one with the really popular lectures, *held his seclusion weeks of meditation, sesshin, pupils from many parts of Japan came to attend.
And during one of the gatherings a pupil was caught stealing.
The matter was reported to Bankei with the request that the culprit be expelled.
Bankei ignored the case.
Later, this student was caught in a similar act.
And again, Bankei disregarded the matter.
This angered the other students.
They drew up a petition asking for the dismissal of the thief, stating that otherwise they would leave in a body.
When Bankei read this petition, he called them before him.
You are wise brothers, he told them.
You know what is right and what is not right.
You may go somewhere else to study if you wish.
But this poor brother does not yet know right from wrong.
Who will teach him if I do not?
I'm going to keep him here even if all the rest of you leave.
A torrent of tears cleansed the face of the brother who had stolen and all desire to steal had vanished.*
Story about great faith, from the teacher.
And it reminded me of another story, which is not exactly what it was saying.
But you remind me of a story from the Russian, Armenian, kind of Armenian, Greek, Russian mystic Gurdjieff.
Do you know about George Gurdjieff?
Anyway, he was an early, I forget, forties, fifties, powerful teacher on the scene.
He had residential communities.
He had one in Paris for a long time and then somewhere else and then back in France.
It was an intense communal scene.
And there was this one person in there that just bugged the heck out of everybody.
Just annoying and difficult to be around.
I forget the kind of things the person did, but just one of these people that just drives you nuts, and everyone just didn't seem to fit in at all.
Why was he even here?
He didn't seem to understand the teachings or the practices they were doing.
It just drove everyone nuts and it was so hard to be patient around this guy.
So finally, a delegation goes to Gurdjieff and says, why is this guy here?
You've got to get rid of him.
He's really messing up the practice and he's making the community intolerable and it's just awful.
Could you just ask him to leave, please?
And Gurdjieff smiles at them and says, I'm paying him to stay here.
So every group needs, it's like the great story about Atisha and his annoying Bengali tea boy, when he goes to Tibet.
So, throwing a few stories out there.
I actually have this on a, no, it's on a Kindle book I can't share with you that easily.
I was going to say I could post these on the website, but I'll do what I can.
I think if those strike you or remind you of anything, have you heard some of those stories before?
And just like the koans, you notice if this stuff exactly happened the way it's said, but written down a lot longer ago than I quite realized, in 1919.
Any comments or thoughts about these stories and family stories in general?
They do seem to serve a certain role, right?
A certain purpose in their lives.
**Participant:** Maybe some things you can only learn through examples.
But I love, oh, go ahead, go ahead.
What I love about the stories is it's a way of allowing the Zen to really get into your bones.
If you just hear him and sit with him, and yeah, I think that's what I want to say about that.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
And they humanize Zen in a certain way too, don't they?
These are people trying their best, with their foibles and problems and eccentricities and exuberances and so on.
**Participant:** It reminded, [unclear: "Branks"] reminded me of Thanksgiving stories, of old family stories around the table.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Right, right, right.
The foibles of grandpa and various other people.
Do you remember any particularly good ones?
**Participant:** Not myself, just now.
It's just that that's the kind of thing, but it's how families get together.
They remember those times when somebody was ridiculous.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Right.
Sometimes they're distorted in amusing ways.
Like one I've been retelling a little bit lately: my family went on a vacation to New England from California, I think, to visit relatives and stuff.
And we rode a ferry across some lake or something, maybe across Lake Michigan or something.
Or maybe it was someplace with islands.
I don't know where it was, but we were riding this ferry and it was me and my brother, my sister hadn't come or hadn't appeared yet.
So we were pretty young, of four and six or six and eight or something like that.
And one of us dropped a rock off the ferry deck and cracked the windshield of a car below.
Yeah.
And I'm pretty sure it was me.
But my mom remembers it as me and my brother.
And my brother was the one who always got in trouble.
And he doesn't remember either way.
So you have no way of knowing really what happened, right?
But was my mom just remembering it the way she thought it should have gone because I was the good kid?
So they tell us stuff about relationships and assumptions and perceptions too, don't they?
These old stories.
It's about stories.
Do you have any good family stories?
**Participant:** When I was very young, my younger brother, two years younger than me, was being changed on the counter in the bathroom.
He was just old enough to roll over, and he rolled over and fell off the counter and broke his jaw.
For about 40 years I believed in my heart of hearts that it had been my job to prevent that from happening, that my mother had somehow told me I was supposed to prevent him from falling.
I told the story to her before she lost her mind to dementia, and she looked at me and said, "I never told you to do that."
So it was just weird.
I have no idea how I processed that it was my fault that my brother's jaw was broken.
But I had that with me for literally about 40 years, until it was finally corrected by my mother when I was sort of telling the story of Thanksgiving.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, it's also the way our stories can be burdens.
Wow.
God, your folks must have felt awful.
Can you imagine?
**Participant:** Oh, dang.
I'm sure my mother carried the guilt with her.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, right.
Yeah.
Your young [unclear: "Ken"] was trying to carry the weight for her.
Yeah.
Well, good stories or thoughts about stories and how they function in our lives?
**Participant:** I think, [unclear: "I get kicked"].
I just think more like we are always running this narrative that we're just all rational and everything makes sense.
But actually, we're more mythic, story based and symbolic.
My grandmother had dementia, and her aunt was taking or my aunt was taking care of her, and her husband, his mother had dementia.
Every Sunday they'd have the two ladies over and they'd have dinner and eat together and tell stories, the same stories, week after week after week.
Then one week my grandmother started telling the other lady's story as if it was her own, and the other lady was nodding her head to it.
And [unclear: "the gene"] and my aunt had a chuckle.
It's also sad, but it's funny, too.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Well, in a way, yeah, like the way we think reality is sort of fixed, in this consensus reality.
But what about when somebody isn't?
Yeah.
**Participant:** When I was a kid, my grandmother lived in the Riverside area, up north, the northern part of Manhattan, and we would go up and have dinner with her, probably once a month.
She was like a perfect Jewish grandmother.
It was like an eight-course meal and all this stuff, and we'd always end up taking stuff home with us.
So there was always this aroma of chicken, because we always went on Fridays.
Right, so it was Shabbos.
I would sit in the back of the car, and for some reason it must have always been a full moon.
We must have gone once a month [unclear: "on the phone"].
Maybe I was six years old, something like that.
You know how when you look out the car window, or a train or something, and you see something in the sky like the moon and it looks like it's moving along with you?
So I would always think that the moon was following us because it wanted some of the chicken.
In my imagination I would be feeding the moon the chicken from my grandmother.
It's one of the few times that I remember something about myself as a child.
When we look at kids and they say something, it's like, oh, my God, as an adult I would never think that.
Right.
Our imaginations become much more fixed.
And that beauty of that open imagination of being a little kid: that's part of why we love stories, too.
We have to reconnect with that childhood imagination.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** That's wonderful.
The moon is following because she wants chicken.
It's just fun, but I think it's really worth paying attention to how stories function in our lives, maybe in ways we don't always even notice.
So thanks for listening and participating and being here.
I appreciate that very much.
